Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

I should have protected others and I failed

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: For a trauma type of trauma to a loved one, the appraisal that the patient's own body has been permanently damaged is hard to reconcile unless the patient also directly sustained major physical injury, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: Avoidance of medical cues can fit some trauma-to-a-loved-one cases, but in this profile it appears to be driven by a personal bodily injury/medical trauma theme that is otherwise unsupported except by the implausible physical-vulnerability appraisal, making this item clinically incoherent with the rest of the profile.

vignette:
Sister Margaret is a 55-year-old woman who has lived in the same Catholic convent for more than two decades, in a rhythm once organized by prayer, communal meals, and visits to the parish school. The event that unsettled that order happened eight months ago, when one of the older sisters, a close friend she had helped care for during a period of declining health, collapsed in a corridor near the small infirmary room. Margaret had been the one to hear the fall. She still remembers the sound of the body hitting the floor and the sight of her friend lying at an angle that immediately felt wrong. Some parts of those minutes are fixed in almost photographic detail—the hem of the sister’s habit twisted beneath her, the smell of floor polish, the cold brightness from the window at the end of the hall—while other moments drop away entirely. She cannot say clearly who called 911 or exactly how long she knelt there, only that she has flashes of pressing at her friend’s shoulder and thinking, with rising panic, that she should have checked on her earlier.

Her account of what happened is saturated with blame. Margaret has come to believe that the death happened because of the way she acted: if she had not delayed, if she had noticed some sign sooner, if she had insisted on more supervision, perhaps her friend would still be alive. What torments her most is the conviction that she failed in a duty that mattered deeply to her, that she should have protected another sister and did not. From there a broader doubt has taken hold. She no longer trusts her own judgment in the simple, ordinary ways she once did; she is certain that when something important depends on her, she will miss what matters. Those beliefs seem to fasten onto the memory itself. The most searing images return with absolute clarity, as if her mind is presenting evidence against her, while the blank stretches feel to her like proof that she cannot even rely on herself to know what happened.

In the months that followed, those memories began arriving without warning. Walking past a polished hallway at the convent, catching the sharp scent of disinfectant outside the infirmary, or hearing a sudden thud during chores could bring back the whole scene instantly, so vividly that for a moment she felt she was back on the floor beside her friend. Because the memory could overtake her so abruptly, she began avoiding the corridor where the collapse occurred, taking a longer route through the building even when it made her late for communal prayer. She also started pulling away from grief reminders more broadly: she leaves quickly if conversation turns to the sister who died, avoids looking at her photograph in the memorial display, and has found reasons not to help sort her belongings. At work in the convent, these maneuvers are now woven into her day so thoroughly that other sisters have noticed how often she volunteers for tasks in distant rooms and declines anything near the infirmary.

Margaret also developed quiet rituals in her head that she does not disclose easily because they feel irrational and shameful. Before bed, before another sister leaves for an appointment, or if an ambulance passes nearby, she repeats set prayers in a particular number and order until it feels “safe enough,” as if failing to do so might allow another catastrophe. These rituals make sense to her because she feels so unable to rely on herself; if her own judgment failed once, she reasons, she must guard against failure in every possible way. Yet the more she depends on these private acts and on steering away from reminders, the more fragile she feels. Each avoided hallway seems to confirm that she cannot bear what happened, and each ritual quietly reinforces the idea that danger will return unless she manages it perfectly.

That pattern has narrowed her world and sharpened the memory rather than softening it. By staying away from the site and from reminders of the sister she lost, she has never had the ordinary repetition that might make the memory feel like something in the past; instead it remains preserved in jagged pieces, either intensely clear or abruptly blank. When it breaks through, it does so with the same force, and Margaret reads that force as further evidence of failure: if she were stronger, if she had done the right thing then and were handling it rightly now, she believes she would not be so vulnerable to it. In turn she doubles down on avoidance and on the mental prayers, trying to prevent another loss and to prevent the memory from taking hold, only to find herself more watchful, more restricted, and less trusting of herself.

Her husband, from whom she has long had a warm but somewhat geographically divided marriage because of religious life and family arrangements, recently told her that every phone call now circles back to the same question of what she should have done differently. What finally brought Margaret to seek help was a recent incident in the convent hallway: a novice dropped a metal tray, and Margaret was instantly back in the moment of finding her friend on the floor. She had to steady herself against the wall, then spent the evening repeating prayers in her room, convinced that something terrible would happen to another sister if she stopped. She comes to treatment frightened that she is becoming someone governed by dread and self-reproach, and hoping, cautiously, that she might learn how to remember her friend without feeling condemned by the memory.
